Once again Clint Eastwood doesn’t simply create a conservative-wet-dream here, even if sometimes in the discourse about this film, the idea might come up; I definitely disagree with the claim, that this is a glorification of the Iraq-war or any US-military operation in the western Asian area of the past 30 years. I think Eastwood simply tells the story of war from the perspective of a “brain-washed” American soldier and thus wants to us see, what someone sees, who was brought up with a rifle in their hands already and frightened by the media, who created the picture of the “dangerous Muslim terrorist” in the minds of Americans after 9/11. The central question to ask is: does Eastwood side with Bradley Cooper’s character or does he just observe his actions. When you think, that he sides with “Chris Kyle”, then this film is on the same territory as something like Michael Bay’s “Pearl Harbour”, where the US-Army is glorified. I don’t think that we are on such territory here. Through the direction and also through Cooper’s performance there is always a distinct rift between the viewer and “Kyle” as a character. Eastwood doesn’t allow us to fully identify with him. He is definitely depicted as a slightly weird guy, who is drawn into the entire topic of war and the horrors, that come with it and who also doesn’t really understand, what his actions really mean; he is someone, who cannot see clear about the horrors, that he commits, which is also why he doesn’t feel sorry. But that doesn’t mean that Eastwood himself wants us to be the same. For me this is — much like other Clint Eastwood movies, whose style of conservative filmmaking is (as I have pointed out recently in my review for “J. Edgar”) much more nuanced — an observers view on a system, where technically we should feel pity for those people, who are unable to see behind the curtain and fall right into the traps. Thus it’s also a bit dull to call this movie out for being too focussed on the American perspective and seemingly uninterested about the casualties that this man creates in Iraq. Eastwood simply doesn’t want to show this here; his focus is the story of a soldier’s life, that is destroyed by a war-machinery, that makes him believe to be heroic part of something, while eventually he’s just ammunition for the interest of someone else — kind of the idea that the first two acts of “Born of the Fourth of July” follows. This is also hauntingly shown, when “Kyle” is back home for a short time and shows his son to use a rifle, just like his father did. The cycle of violence won’t stop here, because these people are trapped in the world of serving someone else’s interests — something that’s incredibly far away from the ideology that I’d associate with Clint Eastwood. So all in all it’s a film about the lost lives of soldiers and as such it succeeds mostly. I decided to still give a rather mid rating, because for me the runtime is too long, especially since the story gets a little repetitive the longer “Kyle” stays in the war-zone. A higher focus on “Kyle’s” family life and the destruction of it would have made a better movie in my opinion, even if Eastwood is able to create some intense fighting scenes. But this should have been more like “The Best Years of our Lives” or “Apocalypse Now” and less like “Warfare”, because there’s no way that I won’t get bored at 130 minutes of people shooting around in the desert.

'MERICA FUCK YEAH American Sniper is probably the most patriotic movie I've ever watched. It doesn't try to hide this fact, constantly pushing the flag loving American way in the viewers face throughout. This movie very much feels like an American propaganda piece. And despite that, for the most part, its a fun action movie. My issues lie with the fact it isn't just that. Chris Kyle's story in this movie is paced pretty poorly. It's not really believable, overly dramatic and romanticised. The movie excels when it focuses less on the American and more on the Sniper. There's just this random shift in the story to try to create compassion for Chris Kyle that just doesn't work, it's too forced and unbelievable. Now the sniping is fun! The action is exciting. The meat of the movie is there. I wish there was a little more focus on the Sniping itself it feels like it was more a vehicle to tell the story through. But there were a few stand out moments. A simple American Propaganda piece. Watch it with that in mind, it can be a good time!

Testosterona, patriotismo, explosiones, Texas, AMÉRICA🦅🦅 Bueno no es tan descarado como en alguna otra película pero se nota claramente la americanada, a pesar de ser una biografía de Chris Kyle, uno de los mejores francotiradores de la historia. A pesar de la simpleza que estas películas suelen tener, aquí se da mucho enfoque a los efectos que los veteranos experimentan tras volver a casa del campo de batalla. Chris está físicamente en Texas, sin embargo, su mente sigue oyendo tiros y helicópteros como cuando estaba en Iraq. Para él, la guerra al principio tuvo un carácter colectivo, se alistó para “defender a su país” y utilizar sus habilidades para proteger al resto de soldados compatriotas; sin embargo, a medida que la película avanza, su misión va adquiriendo un carácter más personal, incluso poniendo en riesgo la vida de sus camaradas y la suya, con el fin de abatir al francotirador enemigo. El hecho de que sea una biografía real es algo interesante, pero a la vez te hace replantearte varias cosas. Las atrocidades que se cometieron en esa guerra (y las que no se muestran) y los efectos que tanto la población civil como los soldados destinados están por sufrir es la mejor propaganda antibelicista del mundo. Al final, la guerra es desmontada por la verdad. Lo que debería haber sido la biografía de un hombre (aunque respetable en muchos aspectos) que ama la guerra, se ha convertido en propaganda en contra de aquello a lo que amaba, algo irónico, ¿no? En conclusión, peli entretenida si tienes un viaje de poco más de dos horas y no has dormido las suficientes horas como para reflexionar bien sobre una película.

Intenso e realistico, con un’interpretazione straordinaria di Bradley Cooper. Il film mostra il lato umano e psicologico di un soldato, rendendo tangibile la pressione e il trauma della guerra. A volte il classico “eroismo militare” viene enfatizzato eccessivamente, ma la narrazione resta concreta e non mitologica.

This movie has an interesting point to make about how difficult it is for soldiers to readjust to normal life after the trauma of war. Unfortunately, that idea never feels fully explored. The perspective on the war is extremely one sided, there are too few moments that really show his struggle outside the battlefield, and the whole thing often feels closer to military glorification than to a deeper reflection on what war takes from a person. Because of that, what could have been a great film ends up feeling just average. PS: The fake baby still haunts me.
